title: Publish to stores
titleHelp: Send your app's Google Play build to your own Google Play developer account, or add it to your own F-Droid repository, without leaving this page.
intro: Connect your own store accounts once, then send each new version from here. Your app is published under your name, on your accounts.
publishFirst: Publish your app first, then make a Google Play build above.
buildFirst: Make a Google Play build above first (the "Google Play (AAB)" card, "Build for Google Play"). Finished builds show up here.
ownerOnly: Only the app's owner can connect store accounts and send apps to stores.
failed: That didn't work. Try again in a moment.
buildHelp: Which Google Play build to send. Every build has its own build number; a store only takes a number it hasn't seen before.

oauth.connected: Your Google Play account is connected.
oauth.cancelled: Google sign-in was cancelled. Nothing was connected.
oauth.expired: That sign-in link expired or was opened in another browser. Try again from this page.
oauth.noScope: Google didn't give permission to manage your Play Console. Sign in again and leave the Google Play box ticked.
oauth.failed: Google sign-in didn't work. Try again, or connect with a service-account key instead.

play.intro: Upload new versions straight to a testing track or to production on your Google Play developer account.
play.disconnectHelp: Forget this account on this site. A Google sign-in is also revoked at Google. Your apps on Google Play are not affected.
play.disconnectConfirm: Disconnect {account}? Your apps stay on Google Play; you just can't send new versions from here until you connect again.
play.signInHelp: Sign in with the Google account that owns (or can manage) your Play Console, and allow access to Google Play. You can disconnect at any time.
play.useKeyHelp: For teams and automation: a key file for a Google Cloud service account that you invite to your Play Console.
play.keyStep1: In Google Cloud Console, create (or pick) a project and turn on the "Google Play Android Developer API".
play.keyStep2: Create a service account in that project, open it, go to Keys and add a JSON key. The .json file downloads.
play.keyStep3: In Play Console, open Users and permissions, invite the service account's email, and give it access to your app with the "Release to production" and "Release apps to testing tracks" permissions.
play.keyStep4: Upload the .json file here. It is stored encrypted and only used to send your apps.
play.keyFileHelp: The JSON key file Google Cloud downloaded for the service account.
play.trackHelp: Internal testing reaches up to 100 testers within minutes. Closed and open testing go to your testers. Production goes to everyone (after Google's review).
play.modeHelp: Release to everyone on the track, roll out to a share of people first, or only prepare a draft that you finish in Play Console.

modes.completed: Release to everyone on the track
modes.draft: Save as a draft in Play Console

play.notesPlaceholder: Shown on Google Play under "What's new". Up to 500 characters.
play.notesHelp: Release notes in English (en-US). Add other languages in Play Console if you want.
play.sendHelp: Uploads the build's app bundle (AAB) to your Google Play account and puts it on the chosen track. Large apps can take a few minutes.
play.sending: Sending to Google Play. You can leave this page; the result shows below.
play.checkHelp: Checks that this account can update this app on Google Play, without changing anything.
play.productionConfirm: This releases the app to everyone on Google Play once Google has reviewed it. Continue?
play.firstUpload: Google needs the very first version of a new app to be uploaded by hand: create the app in Play Console with the package name {app}, download the app bundle (AAB) above and upload it once. After that, send every update from here.

fdroid.intro: Your own F-Droid repository: people add it once in the F-Droid app and get your apps and their updates from there.
fdroid.createHelp: Makes a repository with its own signing key, at a fixed address you can share. It's free and you can add all your apps to it.
fdroid.created: Your F-Droid repository is ready. Add this app to it below.
fdroid.addressHelp: People add this in the F-Droid app (Settings, Repositories, +). The fingerprint at the end lets F-Droid check the repository is really yours.
fdroid.fingerprintHelp: The SHA-256 fingerprint of your repository's signing key. F-Droid shows it when someone adds the repository.
fdroid.pageHelp: A page with your apps and an "Add to F-Droid" button. Share it with the people who should get your apps.
fdroid.openInAppHelp: On an Android phone with F-Droid installed, this opens F-Droid's "add repository" screen.
fdroid.notInRepo: This app isn't in your repository yet.
fdroid.addHelp: Adds the build's signed APK to your repository. People who added your repository get it as an update in F-Droid.
fdroid.removeHelp: Takes every version of this app out of your repository. People who installed it keep it but get no more updates.
fdroid.signingNote: F-Droid installs the APK signed with your app's upload key. Google Play re-signs apps with its own key, so someone who installed the app from Google Play has to uninstall it before installing it from F-Droid (and the other way round).
fdroid.officialSummary: What about the main F-Droid catalogue?
fdroid.official: The main F-Droid catalogue (f-droid.org) has no developer accounts or upload: its volunteers build every app themselves from public, fully open-source code, and they don't accept apps that include Google's libraries for push notifications and install tracking, which this app's native engine uses. A repository of your own is how F-Droid lets anyone publish their apps, and it works in the same F-Droid app.

history.title: Sent to stores
history.draftOnly: Saved as a draft, because this app isn't published on Google Play yet. Finish the release in Play Console.
history.draft: Saved as a draft. Finish the release in Play Console.
history.released: Released on the track. Google reviews new versions before people get them; that usually takes from a few hours to a few days.
history.notSentForReview: Open Play Console and press "Send for review" to finish.

api.ownerOnly: Only the app's owner can do this. Stop acting as this person first.
api.failed: That didn't work. Try again in a moment.
api.tooManyTries: Too many tries. Wait a few minutes and try again.
api.keyTooBig: That file is too big to be a service-account key.
api.chooseKey: Choose the service account's .json key file.
api.googleSignInOff: Google sign-in isn't set up on this server. Connect with a service-account key instead.
api.chooseTrack: Choose a track and a kind of release.
api.badRollout: For a staged rollout, choose a share between 1 and 99%.
api.badClientId: That doesn't look like a Google OAuth client ID (it ends in .apps.googleusercontent.com).

errors.appNotFound: Google Play has no app with this package name in this account yet, or its first version hasn't been uploaded. Create the app in Play Console with exactly this package name and upload the first app bundle (AAB) by hand once.
errors.forbidden: This account isn't allowed to release this app. In Play Console, open Users and permissions and give it access to the app with release permissions.
errors.apiDisabled: The Google Play Android Developer API is turned off for this service account's Google Cloud project. Turn it on in Google Cloud Console, wait a few minutes, and try again.
errors.signInExpired: The Google sign-in for this account no longer works. Disconnect it and connect again.
errors.badKey: Google didn't accept this service-account key. Make sure it's the .json key of a service account that still exists and that the key wasn't deleted.
errors.notAKey: This file isn't a service-account key. Upload the .json key file Google Cloud downloaded for the service account (Keys, Add key, JSON).
errors.versionUsed: Google Play already has a version with this build number. Make a new Google Play build above (it gets the next number) and send that.
errors.wrongKey: Google Play expects this app to be signed with a different upload key. If the app was first published elsewhere, add that keystore under "Your upload key" above, or ask Google to reset the upload key in Play Console.
errors.packageMismatch: The build's package name doesn't match the app on Google Play.
errors.network: Couldn't reach Google. Try again in a moment.
errors.noBuild: That build can't be found any more. Choose another one, or make a new Google Play build.
errors.badApk: The build's APK couldn't be read. Make a new Google Play build and try again.
errors.signFailed: The repository index couldn't be signed. Try again; if it keeps failing, tell the site's operator.
errors.keyMissing: The repository's signing key is missing on the server. Tell the site's operator.
errors.restarted: The server restarted while this was being sent. Send it again.
errors.busy: This app is already being sent to a store. Wait for it to finish.

admin.title: App stores
admin.help: Lets people connect their Google Play developer account by signing in with Google. Without it they can still connect with a service-account key.
admin.body: Optional. With a Google OAuth client, app owners connect Google Play by signing in with Google. Without one, they connect with a service-account key file. F-Droid repositories need no setup.
admin.step1: In Google Cloud Console, create a project and turn on the "Google Play Android Developer API".
admin.step2: Under Google Auth Platform, set up the consent screen (external) and add the scope https://www.googleapis.com/auth/androidpublisher. Google may ask you to verify the app before people outside your test users can sign in.
admin.step3: Create an OAuth client of type "Web application" with this authorized redirect URI:
admin.step4: Paste the client ID and client secret here.
admin.fromEnv: Google sign-in is currently set up from the server's .env file (GOOGLE_PLAY_CLIENT_ID and GOOGLE_PLAY_CLIENT_SECRET). Values saved here take priority.
